problems.location: Concept 2: The Visible-to-Invisible AI Continuum and Learner Agency / block 5
problems.lesson_text: Highly automated tools (`Agents`, `Choosing`, `Sorting`) remove the burden of intermediate decision-making.
problems.source_text: None of the nine below is good or bad on its own. A screen reader and a screening tool can both be the right call or the wrong one. What changes the outcome is whether someone chose it on purpose, and whether the person on the other end knew.
problems.reason: The lesson labels whole AI types as building or displacing capacity by how visible they are, while the source says no type is good or bad in itself and the outcome depends on purposeful choice and awareness.

problems.location: Concept 3: Cognitive Architecture of Retention: Retrieval, Spacing, and Interleaving / block 1
problems.lesson_text: Consensus meta-analyses (Benassi et al., 2014; Dunlosky et al., 2013; Pashler et al., 2007) establish three core practice architectures that optimize retention
problems.source_text: Focus primarily on the slides, with the other two sources being additional information to fill in any gaps or as “fun facts”.
problems.reason: Concepts 3 to 6 and objectives 3 and 4 are built on How People Learn II, so most of the lesson rests on a source the instructions said to use only for gaps and fun facts.

problems.location: Concept 3: Cognitive Architecture of Retention: Retrieval, Spacing, and Interleaving / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Interleaving math problem sets tripled students' capacity to discriminate equation types, whereas blocked practice only highlighted within-category similarities (Carvalho & Goldstone, 2014a; Rohrer et al., 2015).
problems.source_text: They also found that interleaving concepts improved students’ capacity to discriminate among different categories, while blocked practice emphasized similarities within each category.
problems.reason: The source gives no tripling for interleaving; the "nearly tripled" result in How People Learn II belongs to a different perceptual-learning study on translating between graphs and equations.

problems.location: Concept 3: Cognitive Architecture of Retention: Retrieval, Spacing, and Interleaving / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Classroom studies found 2-week spacing intervals superior to massed drill for vocabulary and phonics retention across ages 4 to 76 (Sobel et al., 2011; Cepeda et al., 2006).
problems.source_text: Studies have shown benefits of spaced practice for learners of ages 4 through 76 ... a study of vocabulary learning among fifth graders suggested that a 2-week interval showed the best results (Sobel et al., 2011). ... it is important to note that wider spacing is not necessarily always better.
problems.reason: The 2-week interval comes from one fifth-grade study, and the 4-to-76 age range comes from other spacing studies, so the lesson turns a single finding into a claim across all ages that the source does not make.

problems.location: Exercise 3.1: Deconstructing an instructional training schedule to uncover how spacing, interleaving, and retrieval manage cognitive load and reduce interference / block 2

problems.source_text: not about the source
problems.reason: Concept 3 never teaches interference or cognitive overload and presents these strategies as adding desirable difficulty, yet the exercise and its rubric ask students to justify how they reduce overload and interference.

problems.location: Exercise 5.1: Diagnosing deficit-based assumptions and stereotype threat vulnerabilities within institutional learning environments and performance feedback / block 4
problems.lesson_text: stereotype threat arises when identities are ignored or invalidated, not simply by mentioning them
problems.source_text: African American school-age children perform worse on achievement tests when they are reminded of stereotypes associated with their social group ... To be negatively affected, a person must be exposed to and perceive a potential cue in the environment and be aware of a stereotype about the social group with which he identifies
problems.reason: The source says stereotype threat is triggered by cues that bring a stereotype to mind, not by ignoring identities, so the rubric's "correct" answer contradicts the source and the lesson's own Concept 5 callout.
